evidence.claim: The village, in Kentucky’s Bluegrass region southwest of Lexington, preserves 34 original nineteenth-century buildings and 2,800 acres of farmland.
evidence.quote: Today, with 34 original 19th-century buildings and 2,800 acres (1100 hectares) of farmland

evidence.claim: Pleasant Hill’s Shaker community was active from 1805 to 1910.
evidence.quote: Pleasant Hill in Kentucky, United States, is the site of a Shaker religious community that was active from 1805 to 1910.

evidence.claim: After the society dissolved, the property changed hands and uses, although elderly Shakers remained until Mary Settles died in 1923.
evidence.quote: Following the dissolution of the Shaker society in 1910, the property changed hands several times and was used for a variety of purposes.  Elderly Shakers continued to live on the property until the death in 1923 of Mary Settles, the last Pleasant Hill Believer.

evidence.claim: In 1961, Lexington-area citizens led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace began a restoration effort.
evidence.quote: In 1961, a group of Lexington-area citizens led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace launched an effort to restore the property.

evidence.claim: By 1964, the Friends of Pleasant Hill had secured a federal loan to purchase and restore the site.
evidence.quote: By 1964 the Friends of Pleasant Hill had organized a non-profit corporation, raised funds for operating expenses, and secured a $2 million federal loan to purchase and restore the site.

evidence.claim: Pleasant Hill’s Shakers used horses to pump water into a tower on high ground in the early 1830s.
evidence.quote: in the early 1830s the Shakers of Pleasant Hill constructed a water tower on a high plot of ground. A horse-drawn pump lifted water into the tower

evidence.claim: Pipes carried that water to kitchens, cellars and wash houses, where horse-powered washing machines reduced the work of laundering clothes and linens.
evidence.quote: from there a system of pipes conveyed it to the kitchens, cellars, and wash houses. It is believed to have been the first in the state. In the wash houses, the members built washing machines (also powered by horses) to reduce the heavy work of laundering the community's clothes and linens.

evidence.claim: The village already had large stone and brick dwellings, shops and stone sidewalks by 1825.
evidence.quote: By 1825, the Pleasant Hill Shaker village was a handsome community with large stone and brick dwellings and shops, grassy lawns, and stone sidewalks.

evidence.claim: Its engineering extended to farm work: an elevator moved grain to an upper mill floor, and a mechanical sheller processed corn.
evidence.quote: Their mill had an elevator for moving grain to the upper floor, and they had a mechanical corn sheller.

evidence.claim: Thirty-four original nineteenth-century buildings survive at the village.
evidence.quote: Today, with 34 original 19th-century buildings

evidence.claim: Pleasant Hill’s Meeting House became an automotive garage after the Shaker society dissolved.
evidence.quote: The Meeting House was converted for use as an automotive garage;

evidence.claim: Its wooden floor had been built to withstand several hundred people dancing in worship, and it proved strong enough to support the vehicles driven inside.
evidence.quote: the wood floor, built to withstand the dancing of several hundred brethren and sisters, proved strong enough to support the vehicles driven onto its surface.

evidence.claim: The building later changed use again, becoming a Baptist church.
evidence.quote: Some years later the structure was again converted, this time for use as a Baptist church.
